passage:
I'm Charu, and when the market fell by a fifth last spring, I felt sick opening my account. Everything I owned looked smaller.
My friend Himani asked one question: "When do you need this money?" Not "what should you do", just that.
I took a piece of paper and made two piles. One was my retirement savings, which I won't touch for decades. The other was the deposit for a flat, which I hoped to use in two years. They had sat side by side in my head as one number, and that was the problem.
The first pile could wait out the storm. The second one needed a proper look, maybe with a registered adviser. I still felt uneasy, but for the first time the fear had edges.
— Charu

qa.a: The deposit is meant to wait two years.

qa.a: Charu could talk with a registered adviser to understand the general options for money needed within two years.

qa.a: Himani may have wanted Charu to see the answer through Charu's own goals, since the question itself made the difference.

Workplace financial-wellness session, adviser's note, 14 March.
Pooja came to the drop-in desk looking shaken. Her investments were down about twenty percent since January, and she asked whether she should get out before it got worse.
I did not answer that. I asked when she would need each part of the money. She thought, then split it herself: one part was for a flat deposit she hoped to pay in about two years; the other was for retirement, more than thirty years away.
She worked it through aloud. "The retirement money has decades. This fall isn't what matters for that. But the flat money I might need soon. That's the part I'm actually worried about." We talked in general terms about how people often match money to when it is needed, and she booked a longer session with a registered adviser next week to decide about the flat fund.
— Binita

What was Pooja feeling when she came to the desk?

passage:
Mohit's diary, Friday.
The market is down twenty percent from its peak. My investment app is all red. I nearly sold everything at lunch.
Instead I called Deepika, who works at a bank, and she asked me one annoying question: "When do you need the money?"
I didn't have an answer, so tonight I wrote it down.
Money for my share of the flat deposit: needed in about two years. That's the part that scares me. If it's down twenty percent when I need it, that's real.
Money for retirement: needed in thirty-five years. Honestly, a bad month doesn't mean much for that.
So they're not the same money, and I shouldn't treat them as one red number. Tomorrow I'll call the adviser my bank assigned me and ask specifically about the two-year money. Nothing else. No panic selling tonight.

qa.q: Who did Mohit call instead of selling?
qa.a: Deepika, who works at a bank.

qa.a: Mohit felt panicky and scared, seeing everything in red.

qa.q: What does Mohit plan next, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Calling the adviser about the two-year money only, because that money is needed soon while the retirement money has decades.

qa.q: How does Deepika's question help Mohit?
qa.a: Her question splits one frightening number into money needed soon and money needed decades away.
